implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore is the suspending realization: acquire() suspends the coroutine (never blocking a thread) in FIFO order, release() throws IllegalStateException when it would exceed the permit count, tryAcquire() is the non-suspending form, and withPermit { ... } is the acquire/release pair that releases even when the block throws - the idiomatic encoding of 'release on every exit path'. Use it whenever the callers are coroutines; the blocking java.util.concurrent.Semaphore would pin a dispatcher thread while suspended.
pitfalls: withPermit releases in a finally block, but a permit held across a long suspension still consumes the concurrency budget; keep the critical section short.
The kotlinx semaphore is fair/FIFO by design, so throughput-sensitive paths that prefer barging must use the JUC semaphore instead.
Mixing kotlinx and java.util.concurrent semaphores for the same resource creates two independent counters, and the effective bound is neither number.

variants.name: java.util.concurrent.Semaphore (blocking threads)
variants.implementation_notes: For plain threads, Java interop or code that must block an OS thread, java.util.concurrent.Semaphore is the direct realization: acquire()/tryAcquire(timeout, unit)/release(n) with an optional fairness flag, usable from Kotlin without any coroutine machinery. It is the right choice inside executor tasks and JNI/blocking code, and the wrong one inside a coroutine, where blocking a dispatcher thread defeats the scheduler.
pitfalls: release() is unbounded, so an over-release silently raises the permit count above the constructor value.
Blocking acquire() inside a coroutine pins a dispatcher thread; wrap such calls in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or use the suspending semaphore.
acquire() throws InterruptedException and clears the interrupt flag, which Kotlin code often ignores, losing cancellation.
